niche.title: Why a Doctor Invented the Gatling Gun 🩺
niche.description:
Richard Jordan Gatling earned a medical degree from Ohio Medical College in 1850 but never practiced medicine. During the Civil War he noticed that most soldiers were lost to disease rather than gunshots. In 1861 he designed a gun with six barrels turned by one hand crank, patented on November 4, 1862. In 1877 he wrote that a gun letting one man do as much battle duty as a hundred would reduce the need for large armies, and so exposure to battle and disease. The U.S. Army adopted it in 1866 and declared it obsolete in 1911, after 45 years of service.

Her name may have faded from history—but her story deserves to be remembered.

niche.title: “Boys, This Is Butchery”: The Colonel Who Stopped a Battle to Save His Enemies
niche.description:
The Woods Caught Fire With Wounded Enemies Inside.
June 27, 1864. Kennesaw Mountain, Georgia.
Sherman's assault collapsed in front of the Confederate trenches.
Wounded Union soldiers were left in dry brush between the lines.
Then the brush caught fire.
Lt. Col. William Martin of the 1st Arkansas climbed onto his own earthworks with a white handkerchief.
"Boys, this is butchery."
Both armies stopped shooting and pulled the wounded out together.
A Union officer gave him a pair of pearl-handled Colt revolvers in thanks.
Today a marker stands on that ground. Its title: A Humanitarian Act.

niche.title: Did Civil War Wounds Really Glow?
niche.description:
The “Angel’s Glow” story says some wounded soldiers at Shiloh saw their injuries shine in the dark—and seemed to heal better. In 2001, two students proposed that a glowing soil bacterium, Photorhabdus luminescens, could explain it. The science is plausible, but the Shiloh story itself remains unconfirmed.
